speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MILK-REPORTED FAILURE TO PAY AVERAGE PRICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Agriculture. In view of the fact that a number of persons and organizations are apparently attempting to frustrate the minister's policy of an average price of $4 a hundred for manufactured milk-I am sure the minister is aware of this-could the minister tell the house whether attempts are being made to see that this average price will in fact be maintained?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: MILK-REPORTED FAILURE TO PAY AVERAGE PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my information is that there are complaints with regard to some processors who have raised the price of transportation with respect to milk. The Ontario milk marketing board has set the price at $3.25, and it is apparently felt that this raising of the transportation cost will ultimately result in the producers receiving less than $4. With respect to the cost of transportation, we of course have no control over this, but I sincerely hope the provincial government will take adequate action to make the $3.25 price effective.
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: MILK-REPORTED FAILURE TO PAY AVERAGE PRICE
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I should like to ask the minister what action he proposes to ensure that the producers do receive the amount his government promised to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: MILK-REPORTED FAILURE TO PAY AVERAGE PRICE
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that the federal government has no authority to set the price paid to producers. Our policy enables the price of $3.25 to be paid plus the 75 cents federal payment. The Ontario government in its wisdom through the Ontario milk marketing board set a price of $3.25, which enabled the price of $4 to be paid. If the processors are taking advantage of this improperly, action can no doubt be taken by the Ontario milk marketing board. It cannot be taken by the federal government, which has no authority over transportation costs.

subtopic: MILK-REPORTED FAILURE TO PAY AVERAGE PRICE

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, June 13, consideration in committee of Bill No. S-17, to amend the Bankruptcy Act-Mr. Cardin- Mr. Batten in the chair.
On clause 1-Reviewable transaction.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO CORRECT ABUSES AND FOR ORDERLY PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry? The hon. member for Yukon.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO CORRECT ABUSES AND FOR ORDERLY PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to thank the hon. member for Yukon for giving me the opportunity to speak now; I understand that he had the floor. I also want to apologize to the committee for not being able to be present during the second reading stage of this bill. However, I am happy that we were able to move into the committee stage, where it will be possible to deal generally with the subject of bankruptcy. Like all hon. members I am most anxious for this bill to pass as quickly as possible because, as has been mentioned by hon. members, it is an urgent and most important bill.
The nature and complexity of the problem of bankruptcy make it evident to all hon. members that the amendments to the bill alone will not and cannot solve the problem of what is now termed fraudulent bankruptcies. It is also quite clear that adequate administrative steps are most essential.
Because of the widespread misunderstanding and confusion which exists in the minds of the public with regard to the whole question of bankruptcy, its administration and the law of bankruptcy itself, I believe it is important that a statement be made on all aspects of the subject of bankruptcy at this time. I hope members of the committee will bear with me if I go not only into the reasons behind the principal amendments to the Bankruptcy Act, but also if I describe briefly the steps that have been taken and that must still be taken if in fact we are going to ensure that the administration and control of bankruptcy legislation is adequate to meet the problem that now faces the country in this field. I want to assure the committee that I will be as quick as I can, but I think it is important that a comprehensive statement be made.
In recent months many accusations and allegations have been levelled against the federal government in this field. I believe that all hon. members as well as all Canadians ought to know what actions and

June 16, 1966
Bankruptcy Act
steps have been taken to face up to the problems that have developed in this field over the years, particularly actions that have been taken since the appointment of the new superintendent in April, 1965. I believe this is necessary not only to show that we are aware of the problems and that we have been and still are taking the necessary measures to deal with them, but also to give a good measure of reassurance to the country and especially to those in the business and commercial sections of the community.
There is no doubt in my mind-and I trust that hon. members will share my conviction after they have heard what I have to say- that the changes now contemplated will permit the superintendent to deal much more effectively with the bankruptcy problem and with the flagrant abuse which is made of the present bankruptcy legislation.
In this respect I should like to say a word, first of all, about the important aspect of federal-provincial co-operation in the field of bankruptcy. At the last conference of attorneys general held in Ottawa in early January of this year there was a frank and open discussion of the problems relating to the administration of the bankruptcy legislation. The experience of both the provincial and the federal authorities in this field was discussed, and I am sure no hon. member will be surprised to hear me state that the conference agreed that an adequate and effective system of administration of estates in bankruptcy and the prevention of irregularities depend upon the action of both the federal and provincial governments operating in their respective fields of responsibility, and upon appropriate co-operation between them.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
It would be wrong for anyone to conclude that there was a lack of co-operation in this field between the two levels of government. This is not the case. But this means that the co-operation that has existed in recent years ought to be organized in a more ordinate, articulate and systematic manner. As a consequence the conference set up a small committee comprising the deputy attorneys general of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec and the superintendent to study means of achieving closer co-operation between the federal and provincial authorities.
This committee has met and a procedure has been established whereby both the provincial law enforcement authorities and the superintendent of bankruptcy will be in constant and close liaison. The superintendent of

bankruptcy is presently in communication with the deputy attorneys general of the other provinces, and I do not think there should be any reason why the arrangements regarding the provinces of Ontario and Quebec should not be extended with the other provinces.
I think hon. members will be interested to know, in concrete cases, how the arrangements could work and what kinds of benefits could be derived therefrom. I will mention one example without being specific as to names, places or dates, because this information is taken from an active file.
The trustee of a large estate in bankruptcy came to Ottawa to meet with the superintendent. The trustee explained that he strongly suspected that in the few months preceding his bankruptcy, the bankrupt had fraudulently diverted some funds belonging to the estate to the United States, and that the bankrupt was about to abscond from Canada. The superintendent immediately got in touch with the R.C.M. Police with the request that the trustee be afforded all the necessary assistance in his investigation of the affairs of the bankrupt. This was done. At the same time the superintendent got in touch with the department of the attorney general of the province concerned and arrangements were made to have a crown attorney appointed right at that stage to handle any criminal prosecution that could ensue.
The suspicions of the trustee proved to be well founded. When the bankrupt was about to leave the country for good he was charged, arrested and brought before the court where he is now awaiting trial. This was possible because of the close liaison and co-operation that existed with the trustee as well as between the provincial and federal authorities. There are also good possibilities that as a result of the investigation, the estate will be in a position to recover some of the assets that had been illegally taken out of the country, this to the benefit of the creditors of the estate.
This is but one example pointing up the close liaison that has been established between the provincial and federal authorities, both operating in their own spheres of responsibilities; and I am convinced that hon. members will agree with me that this is a most important achievement.
I must at this point say a word about the spheres of responsibility of the federal and provincial governments in this field. At the
June 16. 1966

conference of the attorneys general the experience of both the federal and provincial authorities, especially in the field of the enforcement of the provisions of the Criminal Code dealing with frauds and other similar offences having some connection with bankruptcies, was reviewed. It was the consensus that the arrangements that resulted from the 1949 act were no longer adequate to deal with the problems that we have to face today.
Of course I do not need to emphasize the point. Bankruptcy and insolvency, under our constitution, is a subject matter of federal legislative jurisdiction, while the administration of justice in the province is a subject matter of provincial legislative jurisdiction. It follows that the investigation and prosecution of fraudulent transactions committed before a bankruptcy are the responsibility of the provincial authorities in the course of the ordinary administration of criminal justice. Even fraud on the part of the trustee falls within the field of provincial responsibility for the administration of criminal justice, although the superintendent is obviously very interested here from the standpoint of disciplinary action and cancellation of the trustee's licence. He may, therefore-and he does in fact-himself investigate, under the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act, charges against a trustee whose administration has been impugned, and in so doing he may often be in a position to give assistance to the provincial law enforcement authorities.
Hon. members are aware that our bankruptcy legislation, like that of other countries, is predicated on the principle of creditor control. Many provisions of the act can be traced to this underlying principle, such as, for example, the provision whereby the trustee should be appointed having regard to the wishes of the creditors, or the provision dealing with the inspectors of the estate who, as representatives of the creditors, assist the trustee in the discharge of his duties.
The important thing, however, for our present purpose is that creditor's control also means that the responsibility for detecting and eradicating irregularities on the part of bankrupts is the prime responsibility of creditors. The trustee has important responsibilities under the act in that respect and he, as well as the creditors, has the necessary powers to enable him to discharge them adequately.
However, in too many cases the trustee is unable to carry out the necessary investigations because of a lack of funds, and too often
Bankruptcy Act
the creditors are not prepared to provide the trustee with their financial assistance because, as they say, they are not interested in throwing good money after bad. It would not be reasonable to blame the creditors for this attitude. They are of course primarily concerned with minimizing their own losses. At the same time, however, it must be appreciated that this attitude does not meet the long term public requirements in detecting and eradicating irregularities.
In these cases the provincial authorities may be asked by the trustee or the creditors to make some investigation into the affairs of the bankrupt. Such requests should be in line with the constitutional position to which I have just referred. However, there is a serious problem area comprising cases where there is some reason to suspect irregularities but where the creditors, on the one hand, are not prepared to undertake the expense of making an investigation and where the provincial crown prosecutor, on the other hand, does not feel that the suspicion of misconduct is strong enough to bring him into the case at that stage.
This is an area where experience indicates
that the principle of creditor control is not working effectively. At the conference the federal government informed the provincial authorities that it was prepared to take the necessary steps, by way of amendment and otherwise, to enable the superintendent tc conduct investigations in this problem area and carry them to the point where suspicion of irregularity is either dispelled or brought to a degree of concreteness where the crown prosecutor or local police may be expected to interest themselves in the case. The provinces have agreed, on their part, to take up the investigation and prosecution in all cases where the evidence, originally or as a result of investigation instigated by the superintendent, will so warrant.
Clause 3 of the bill which will incorporate new section 3A in the Bankruptcy Act gives increased powers to the superintendent to make investigations and inquiries in respect of these cases that fall within the problem area that I have just referred to.
I have just said that the provincial authorities have some responsibilities in the field of pre-bankruptcy fraud, responsibilities that they do not deny; and I do not think it would be out of place to mention here the special interests that the provincial authorities have taken in the discharge of their responsibilities in this field.

June 16, 1966
Bankruptcy Act
The recent steps that we have taken in
co-operation with the provinces to deal with the problem of pre-bankruptcy frauds or planned bankruptcies will do a great deal to improve the situation on that count.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
However, I do not wish anyone to get the impression that the problem of credit frauds or planned bankruptcies is a simple one. It is not, and unfortunately this is so not only in Canada. It is a problem that other countries, especially the United States, have to face as well. I want to stress, however, that we know the problem and that we are taking concrete steps to cope with it and to provide our honest law-abiding citizens with the protection they need in their business dealings.
At the same time everyone must appreciate that this is no reason to be complacent. The best protection that creditors can get is still and will always be sound credit practices. The creditor who sells on credit to anyone whatever the risk, on a dearth of information as to the purchaser's ability to pay the purchase price, simply because he does not want to lose a sale, is bound to get into trouble.
While it is the public authorities' duty to expose offences and irregularities whenever they occur, there is no assurance that the pursuit of these objectives will permit creditors to recoup their losses in all cases. This is far from being certain, and we must not be mistaken as to the actual effect that these arrangements will have in general in individual cases. Creditors will always best serve their interest by alertly controlling their credit.
To deal effectively with this problem, the provincial and federal authorities have joined their efforts and pulled their forces together. This alliance, however, will not be complete unless creditors join in our efforts to stamp out these dishonest practices. They must themselves reassess if necessary their position vis-a-vis this problem and take steps to protect adequately their interest.
This discussion of problems regarding the investigation and prosecution of frauds or other ordinary criminal offences such as perjury brings me to another problem, and that is the enforcement of those provisions of the Bankruptcy Act that create offences directly related to its administration. For example, it is an offence for a bankrupt to fail to disclose his assets to the trustee, or to fail to present himself for examination before the court, or to fail to prepare and submit to the trustee a statement of his affairs.

The act provides that when the bankruptcy court is satisfied, upon the representations of the superintendent, official receiver or trustee, or any creditor or inspector, that there is ground to believe that an offence has been committed under the Bankruptcy Act or the Criminal Code in connection with a bankruptcy, the court may authorize the trustee to initiate a prosecution. Where a trustee is so authorized either by the creditors, the inspectors or the court, he is required to institute the proceedings and to refer the matter to the local provincial crown attorney.
This is another area where experience has shown that the machinery provided by the 1949 act to deal with offences of an administrative character is not adequate. Experience has shown that in too many cases bankrupts would disregard the requirements of the act and, although the trustee may have reported the offence to the court, nothing would be done with a view to pursuing the matter. This, you will agree, is most unfortunate, but on the other hand should not be too surprising if one considers that the courts do not have the administrative machinery to deal with this type of problem.
Although there are not statistics as to the number of such offences, there are indications that they are far too many and that the lack of prosecutions in these cases has to some extent contributed to an unfortunate laisser-aller attitude in this area and facilitated the operations of those individuals who want to use bankruptcy legislation for purposes other than those that have been ascribed to it by parliament.
There is another area where the federal government has decided to step in. While these offences may still be pursued by the trustee at the instance of the creditors, in the future the superintendent in proper cases, if the matter is not pursued by the trustee, will take the initiative. The prosecutions when initiated by the superintendent will be conducted by counsel in the Department of Justice. In this way we hope to tighten up the administration of the act and make sure that debtors who seek the benefits that flow from bankruptcy will submit themselves to the various requirements of the act.
One of the cornerstones of our bankruptcy legislation, as hon. members know, is the trustee. Only persons who have been licensed by the superintendent under the authority of the Minister of Justice may, as a rule, be appointed to administer estates under the
June 16, 1966

Bankruptcy Act. Trustees are the cornerstone of our bankruptcy system, but from time to time some have been a cause of considerable concern. This, it must be appreciated, is not by any means a new problem.
Back in 1932 parliament introduced the licensing of trustees system because of the abuses that had been uncovered in the administration of estates in bankruptcy. In the same year parliament for the same reason created the office of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy to supervise the trustees administration. I would assume that this legislation resulted in some improvements, but in the late fifties other abuses were reported which resulted in a large number of investigations and prosecutions as well as the suspension and cancellation of a number of trustees' licences.
It was felt necessary at that time to arrange for an auditing of all the trustees in bankruptcy. However, it was only in April of 1964 that the first systematic and periodic audit of trustees was put into effect as the result of an arrangement between the superintendent and the audit services of the comptroller of the treasury of the Department of Finance.

licences have been revoked. I cannot say they have been revoked because of considerations or evidence contained in the Mercier report but some trustees' licences have been revoked.
Arrangements were also made to have the R.C.M. Police carry out a field investigation of all applicants for a licence. At the same time the R.C.M. Police continued to be extensively used in investigations of and spot checks on the trustees' administration. The results of these arrangements, although assuredly they brought about some improvement, were not as satisfactory as had been expected. To continue our policy of improvement we had to look for other solutions and approaches to the problem.
Bankruptcy Act
I sincerely believe that we will not be in a
position to improve on the situation by anything falling short of requiring applicants to submit to a formal examination before a board. However, the policy regarding the licensing of trustees is obviously one of the questions that the revision committee, which has recently been set up to assist with the revision of the Bankruptcy Act, will carefully consider. I am sure that not only will the policy regarding the licensing of trustees be carefully considered but that the advisability of establishing a system of some sort of public trustees, as exists in England and Australia, will be one of the questions that the committee will look into.
In the meantime I do not intend to authorize the appointment of new trustees save possibly in very exceptional cases where the public interest might be involved. So far I have received no indication that the fact that no new trustees have been appointed in the last 14 months has caused any prejudice to the public.
In so far as present licensees are concerned, we have continued to exercise close surveillance on their administration. Since the month of April 1965-and perhaps this will answer the question posed by the hon. member for Yukon-five licences were either cancelled or not renewed for cause.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO CORRECT ABUSES AND FOR ORDERLY PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext: Would it be not in the public interest to disclose the names of the trustees who lost their licences? If that is so, then I do not insist on an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO CORRECT ABUSES AND FOR ORDERLY PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext:
I could indicate what trustees have lost their licences but I am not sure that this would do anyone any good because they no longer practice in that particular profession and some of them are before the courts. Furthermore, a large number of licences were also renewed at the end of 1965 for the sole purpose of permitting the trustees concerned to dispose of the estates in their hands. The positions of some of these trustees have since been reviewed and a number of restrictions have been lifted. Two former trustees have recently been brought before the courts on charges of misappropriation of funds. One has pleaded guilty and was sentenced last Friday to two years imprisonment; the other is awaiting his trial.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
If we have taken strong action to eliminate the undesirable individuals from the ranks of the trustees we also at the same time have

June 16, 1966
Bankruptcy Act
recently implemented a number of measures to assist them in providing a still better service to the community. I shall elaborate on that in a moment. I have said that trustees are the cornerstone of our bankruptcy administration system. The superintendent, on the other hand, is now the keystone of the entire system. This is so, of course, because of the key role he plays in the surveillance of the administration of all estates in bankruptcy and also because of his increased responsibilities regarding the pre-bankruptcy problem area to which I referred a moment ago.
Furthermore, I believe that the Superintendent of Bankruptcy is in a position to show the way to the other officials concerned with bankruptcy administration. Of course, in order to assume this leadership the superintendent needs a sufficient supporting staff. Hon. members might be interested to know in that respect that from 1958 to 1962 the establishment of the office of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy provided for 11 positions, including two positions of auditors. In 1962 two more positions of auditors were created. In 1964 the positions of assistant superintendent and office manager were created. In September of 1965 the number of auditor positions was doubled and brought to eight. In November of the same year two new positions providing for a bankruptcy officer having residence in each of the cities of Montreal and Toronto were created. This was the first time that the office of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy had on its permanent staff officials operating outside Ottawa.
Therefore, while in 1961 there were 11 positions in the office of the superintendent, this has now been increased to 31. This in my view is an achievement that deserves mention, but hon. members must know that we do not consider the superintendent's office will be able to assume the task that is expected of it without further changes in its establishment.
Just yesterday approval was given for a major reorganization of the office of the superintendent by providing for a considerable enlargement of the skeleton offices already operating in Montreal and Toronto and by opening up an office in Vancouver. The Vancouver office would look after the province of British Columbia as well as the other three western provinces. The Montreal office would take care of the province of Quebec and the Maritime provinces as well. It is intended that each of these offices will comprise auditors and investigators. We are also

contemplating the creation of two positions of deputy superintendent to assist the superintendent.
The proposed arrangements will permit a still closer surveillance of the trustees' administration through auditors and investigators especially trained by and under the direct control of the superintendent's office. They will also permit an effective enforcement of the provisions of the act creating offences of an administrative character. It is intended, furthermore, that the auditors on the staff of the superintendent will be available to assist the R.C.M. Police in their investigations regarding pre-bankruptcy frauds.
Other measures which also have been taken or are contemplated by the department are:
First, the appointment of a judge of the superior court for the Montreal district to sit full time on bankruptcy matters.
Second, the preparation and circulation of bulletins to the trustees to assist them in providing a better performance in uniformiz-ing procedure, in better understanding the various requirements of the act and so on. Two of these bulletins have already been circulated and others are in the course of preparation.
Third, we propose to organize seminars for registrars and official receivers with a view to permitting exchanges of experience, discussion of problems of mutual concern, standardization of procedures and so on. The superintendent is already in contact with the provincial authorities with a view to exploring this project further.
Fourth, we are also exploring the possibility of preparing a kind of code of procedure for official receivers and registrars.
Fifth, we propose to review our statistics program. It is obvious that we will have to put into effect a revised program that will permit the collection of all of the statistics that the competent authorities need to assess the problem areas in the field of bankruptcy. Our statistics program, as it stands now, contributes very little in that respect.
To sum up, the department, as I have said in my opening remarks, has taken, I think, practical and effective steps to cope with the developments that have been taking place in the field. I should like, however, at this point to emphasize that specific cases of irregularities are dealt with immediately they are detected and in that respect we have, as I have just said, improved and are still improving our means of detection. What we are in
June 16, 1966

need of at this point is the co-operation of all civic-minded citizens. We need to be provided with any available information pointing to irregularities or offences so that they may be dealt with within the framework that I have described a moment ago. The task of the department working alone is not easy. Against the unholy alliance of the dishonest debtors, unscrupulous businessmen and unethical lawyers and accountants, we must present the alignment of all of the forces, the civic-minded citizens, the bankruptcy courts and the Department of Justice, all working together in a spirit of co-operation and collaboration for greater integrity of the bankruptcy proceedings. It is in that spirit that I urge anyone who has information pointing to irregularities on the part of trustees or others to come forward and lay this information before us so that we can immediately look into it and, if necessary, launch the appropriate investigations.
I have dealt up until this point with the different steps that we have taken to [DOT]continue our policy of improvements in the administration of the present Bankruptcy Act. We have looked carefully at the legislation itself and it is obvious that it can and should be improved to meet the problems that changes in our society have brought in recent years. Bill S-17 which we are now considering is not a revision of the Bankruptcy Act. As hon. members know, a committee of three members has recently been appointed to assist with a thorough revision of bankruptcy legislation. Since the last revision of the act in 1949 a very large number of representations for amendment to the act have been received from various individuals and organizations, including leading commercial, business and professional associations. A great amount of work had already been done in the Department of Justice toward a complete revision of the act and the assistance provided by the committee on the revision should accelerate the completion of this important and difficult task.
Bill S-17 is an interim measure designed to provide an immediate remedy to some of the most urgent areas of complaint. A number of high priority amendments have therefore been incorporated into this bill and, should they be adopted, I believe they will do a great deal to correct some of the most flagrant abuses of the bankruptcy process. The bill had been very carefully considered by the standing committee on banking and commerce of the other place. As a result a number of changes
Bankruptcy Act
were made to the bill and these changes, with one exception with which I shall deal in a moment, are acceptable to the government. I will have myself three possible changes to bring to the attention of the committee.
I should like to deal briefly with the high priority amendments to which I have just referred because I feel they are most important. One of the most important clauses of this bill is clause 3, to which I have already alluded. It will give increased powers to the superintendent to make investigations and inquiries in respect of those cases that fall within the problem area to which I have just referred. The amendment especially enables the superintendent, with the approval of the court, to search premises for documents that may afford evidence as to an offence in connection with a bankruptcy, to examine such documents and to make copies. Whenever the superintendent obtains evidence of an offence of a criminal nature he will report the matter to the provincial authorities.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
In the other place-and this I should like hon. members to note-a new subsection was added to section 3A incorporating by reference section 126A of the Income Tax Act dealing with the solicitor-client privilege. Under section 126A of the Income Tax Act the document in respect of which the privilege is clamied must be put in a sealed envelope without examination and without making copies. An application must then be made to a judge to determine whether the privilege exists. This procedure applied to the investigation of bankruptcy irregularities would, it is believed, frustrate the investigation. The purpose of examining documents would in many cases be to ascertain who are involved in a suspected fraud connected with a bankruptcy and what the relationship between them may be. This would not be possible if the documents must be sealed up and cannot even be examined. By the time they can be examined it may be that documents in the possession of the persons involved would be gone. If they can be examined immediately then it might well be possible to make a search in other places before there has been an opportunity of destroying or concealing records. Assessment for income tax is a more leisurely process and it must also be borne in mind that we are dealing here with offences and not assessments for income tax.
In the investigation of offences time is of the essence and it may very well be that an

June 16, 1966
Bankruptcy Act
investigation can be completely frustrated if a solicitor-client privilege is asserted and the procedure outlined in the Income Tax Act has to be followed. Moreover, it may well operate as a protection to wrongdoers. Companies carrying on an unlawful enterprise could leave their damaging documents with their solicitor and in that way secure some protection against investigation of their activities.
I am sure that hon. members will give particular attention to this change and consider whether this protection is necessary and warranted, bearing in mind that it is necessary and essential that the superintendent's powers of investigation and examination be resorted to without undue interference. When we come to the appropriate time I propose to introduce an amendment which would in effect drop the change that was brought in by the other place.
Another important amendment has to do with reviewable transactions. We have received numerous representations in recent years regarding certain transactions involving related persons or a closely held corporation and its directors or shareholders in contemplation of bankruptcy. For example, in contemplation of bankruptcy the corporation would pay exorbitant salaries or expense allowances to officers of the company, or the debtor would sell at an unreasonably low price some of his assets to persons or corporations who in some way control the debtor. While transactions of this kind may, under the present state of the law, be legal they do not on many occasions come within what may be called moral business practice.
The amendments-clauses 1 and 12 of the bill-incorporate in the Bankruptcy Act the concept of "at arm's length" which is used in income tax matters. The court will have the power, on the application of the trustee, to review transactions between the debtor and related persons that have taken place within the 12 months preceding the bankruptcy. If the court finds, after having inquired into the matter, that the consideration for the transaction was conspicuously excessive or inadequate, it will give judgment to the trustee for the difference between such consideration and the fair market value of the property or services.
The bill also provides that where a corporation within 12 months preceding its bankruptcy has redeemed shares or granted a dividend when the corporation was insolvent or that it rendered the corporation insolvent,

recovery may be made against the directors or against certain of the shareholders of the bankrupt corporation. Other provisions of the act are amended to restrict the rights of creditors that are related to the bankrupt.
One of the substantial changes that was made to the Bankruptcy Act in 1949 dealt with proposals made by insolvent persons. While it appears that these provisions have been of considerable benefit to debtors and creditors alike, these amendments will eliminate the possibility of abuses by giving the creditors, under the direction of the court, more control over the assets of the debtor. They will also provide that if the proposal is not accepted by the creditors or by the court, the debtor will be deemed to have made an assignment on the date the proposal was originally filed with the official receiver. Likewise, if a proposal is not followed through by the debtor he will be deemed to have made an assignment in bankruptcy.
Other amendments clearly set out a procedure whereby bankrupts may be required to contribute some part of their post-bankruptcy income to the trustee for the benefit of the creditors. The present act would seem to indicate that a contribution may be required but this has been left to the discretion of trustees and the courts with the result that debtors are treated in a most inconsistent manner across the country.
It is often alleged that certain trustees would inform the debtors that they must pay a certain sum to cover the trustee's disbursements and fees, whereupon they would presumably get their discharge. It is also alleged that there are in numerous cases no attempts on the part of the trustee to collect a portion of the debtor's remuneration.
With this amendment the trustee will have the obligation, when directed by the inspectors or the creditors, to see that the debtor deposits for the benefit of his creditors a certain portion of his salary, wages or other remuneration. It is thought that these provisions will prevent the obtaining of a too easy discharge from personal debts through bankruptcy proceedings. As hon. members know, there are a considerable number of other amendments which were referred to very ably by the Solicitor General the other day and I do not propose to repeat what he said.
However, I should like to remind hon. members that this bill does not purport to provide an answer to all of the problems that the representations that were received have raised. Hon. members will appreciate, I am
June 16, 1966

sure, that the numerous representations that were received touch upon almost all the sections of the Bankruptcy Act, which of course are now being reviewed by the revision committee. I need not at this time review these representations but hon. members might be interested to hear about some of the problems that were raised and which are being considered by the committee.
One of the problems, of course, has to do with the easiness with which debtors in certain cases can obtain a discharge from their liabilities. The manner in which bankrupts are being dealt with by the courts no doubt needs to be completely reappraised and the provisions of the present act carefully looked into. This is a problem that has been a cause of some concern, I am informed, in England and Australia and the committees that have been charged by the governments of these countries to recommend amendments to the bankruptcy legislation have made recommendations for substantial changes in that area. This is a problem on which recommendations from our committee to assist in the revision of the Bankruptcy Act will be most helpful.
Another area which will have to be most carefully looked into has to do with the structure of the bankruptcy court itself. Under the present legislative and administrative arrangements the official receivers, although appointed by the governor in council, are in practice employees of the provincial authorities. These authorities will look after the official receivers' remuneration and provide them with the required facilities. The registrars of the courts on the other hand are appointed by the chief justice of the court having superior jurisdiction in the province. In practice, again the registrars are employees of the provincial authorities from whom they receive their remuneration and are provided with the required facilities. These arrangements leave much to be desired and we will be most interested to know what the committee has to say in that respect.
I am inclined myself to feel that the most serious consideration should be given to the advisability of giving exclusive bankruptcy jurisdiction to the Exchequer Court of Canada. I do not intend here to show what benefits would be derived from the giving of exclusive bankruptcy jurisdiction to a court such as the Exchequer Court, and I have no doubt that substantial changes would have to be made in the organization of that court to enable it effectively to assume that jurisdiction. The committee will undoubtedly look into this possibility.

speechtext:
I hope too that these squads will go into some of the existing files in the superintendent's office with respect to which investigations were requested and promised several years ago but have not been conducted to this date.
The seminars for the education of officials mentioned by the minister are an important and helpful addition to the approach to fraudulent bankruptcies. Not only are seminars necessary for the eduction of officials administering the act but some kind of informational effort should be made within the department to inform the public. All sorts of efforts are being made by organizations such as better business bureaux and the Canadian Credit Mens' Association Limited to keep the public informed of rackets involving door-to-door salesman and similar schemes. I do not go along with the minister when he says that the creditor is primarily taken in because of his eagerness to make a purchase. The minister knows how sophisticated these fraudulent operators are. One instance that leaps to my mind immediately is where a dummy corporation obtains an unlisted telephone number through three or four different interveners and then sends out a circular letter, not only to Canada but to other places, soliciting the purchase of commercial goods.
Often these operators give the telephone number of a so-called banker whom creditors can get in touch with should they want a reference. The unlisted number, of course, leads to a basement room in some apartment and a man sits there waiting for a telephone call. When the call comes he knows what he must answer. He has only to say one thing, namely, "Royal Bank", or "Bank of Montreal", or whatever other bank he chooses. The legitimate supplier says he wants to sell so many thousand dollars worth of product X. "What sort of credit rating has the company in question got?" The answer is: "Oh, marvellous. They are good depositors and always discharge their obligations." So the legitimate supplier hangs up, well satisfied that he has been speaking with an official of the bank.

Instead he has been talking to a dummy corporation.
We cannot blame the creditor for being so eager for a sale that he does not check out to the last degree. He checks as far as he can go. The only way in which such operations are going to be disbanded is by preventing the same individuals who operate in this way over and over again using either the facade of corporate liability or the convenience of being able to dump their nom de pret after 60 or 90 days. That can only be done on a centralized basis.
This brings up another area of federal responsibility. I am not sure of the constitutionality of what I am about to say in this regard because I have not done any research in depth. Surely there must be centralized responsibility for preventing the international traffic in commercial wares for fraudulent purposes.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say at the outset that I support wholeheartedly the previous speaker's views, contrary to what the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. 'Nielsen) said, that a royal commission on fraudulent bankruptcies would be totally useless. The problem is well known; it is not a question of crying over what happened in the past but of taking steps to remedy the present situation.
As announced by the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell) last Monday night, when moving second reading of Bill S-17, and as mentioned earlier today by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin), this is an interim measure which is

introduced immediately to put a stop to certain abuses which have been noticed for a long time with regard to bankruptcies.
I regret that it has been impossible to propose immediately a complete revision of the Bankruptcy Act which has not been amended or changed since 1949, but I know that such a step will not be long in coming now.
As a matter of fact, for many years the population, the newspapers and a number of professional and intermediary associations have been asking the various successive governments, at the federal as well as the provincial level, to take all necessary steps to correct the present system and, as far as the federal government is concerned, to amend the Bankruptcy Act. It is not that the legislation itself is bad. In theory it might be excellent but in practice it does not meet and has not met the needs; therefore, it must be amended to suit the situation.
I must congratulate the present Minister of Justice who has finally introduced a bill which should improve things considerably although I deplore the fact that the complete revision of the act has been postponed. Until now, the present minister has certainly taken positive measures to meet the situation, as he mentioned a little earlier; I am thinking in particular of the appointment of a full time superior court judge in Montreal, the increase in staff at the office of the superintendent of bankruptcies, the sending of representatives in Montreal and Toronto and other steps which he mentioned himself a while ago.
The Bankruptcy Act is an important part, I would say an essential part, of our economic life. It is important that this legislation should keep pace with our modern economic world and meet its requirement, and I hope that the three-member commission created recently will soon make recommendations because the act in general still needs to be amended.
This legislation seeks to solve the most urgent problems. During the last war and several years afterwards, bankruptcies or assignments were not very numerous but since 1950 they have increased every year and, as a necessary corollary, the number of fraudulent bankruptcies have also increased. I will not take the time of the committee to give statistics on the number of bankruptcies; they are well known and I am sure that all hon. members are convinced of the importance, the urgency and the need to take the necessary action to fight with all possible means that social and economic evil.
June 16, 1966

The Mercier commission set up by the government of Quebec by Order in Council dated October 16, 1964, set forth in its report tabled in July 1965 what all those who, like me, in their experience, have known for a long time, that dishonesty, fraud and blackmailing were involved in many cases of bankruptcies, and that certain undesirable elements of the population had thus realized fantastic gains, often to the detriment of bona fide creditors, and the federal and provincial treasury. It is time that something be done to correct this intolerable situation which has spread throughout the country.
As many other members, I called, here and elsewhere, for major amendments to the present act, which proved inadequate to correct the abuses disclosed since a few years in that field. The administration of the act comes under the federal government, but the prosecutions come under the provincial government; there may not have been in the past enough co-operation between these jurisdictions.
Nobody will blame the governments if they join forces, as was suggested lately, to strike a lethal blow at the underworld and at the gangdom who batten on fraudulent bankruptcies. However, we need more than halfmeasures to succeed.
As I said a moment ago, the federal government has already taken certain actions which have been mentioned by the Minister of Justice, and I hope that the new superintendent of bankruptcies, with the additional powers given to him by the present act, will be able to exert a closer control over bankruptcies, especially if he is granted a competent, devoted and determined staff, who understand their duties. Expert investigators are necessary to go to the heart of the matter; very often they will have to deal with unscrupulous, dishonest people, who know the means to avert the law and superficial inquiries.
As all new legislation, in the matter of bankruptcies, this act has two main objectives: first, discharge a debtor who is no longer solvent because of unforseen circumstances beyond his control, and second, to allow for a better use or equitable realization of his properties, according to the creditors' rights.
Contrary to what used to be, when only trades people went bankrupt, nowadays the act applies to nearly everybody: big or small businesses, corporations or individuals, independent people or wage-earners. There are also
Bankruptcy Act
various classes of creditors, classes which often are no better off than the bankrupt himself.
All the range of bankruptcies must be taken into consideration. The present act provides improvements requested many times, especially by the bar and various professional bodies, and it certainly fills many gaps.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
But any improvement of the Bankruptcy Act will be meaningless, unless steps are taken to strengthen its administration and application. That is essential; it is the key to the whole matter. And where the application of the act is concerned, the trustee obviously plays the leading role, without for that matter diminishing the role the creditors must play, even though they do not always play it. I do not want to attack all trustees, because most of them, at least I hope so, fulfil their role in protecting the interests of the creditors; but, unfortunately, too many of them forget it and, under the present circumstances, nothing else can be expected.
As a rule, debtors who resort to the Bankruptcy Act want to be freed of their debts under the best terms possible. There is no doubt that insolvency often results from uncontrollable circumstances and it is fair and desirable that the debtor be given a chance to start again in business, free from any obligations which might keep him from doing so. However, the number of bankruptcies is out of proportion with the justifiable cases. The trustee is considered by the debtors-and the trustee quite often considers himself-as the one who is supposed to obtain the discharge, instead of being the administrator of the assets of the bankrupt in the best interest of the creditors. It is natural and human for him to act in the interest of the one who hires and pays him. Man cannot serve two masters. As long as trustees are chosen by the debtors, as is generally the case now, they will be selected for the advantages they will bring their employers, namely the debtors.
The trustees who act otherwise are liable to lose their clients. Moreover, as I mentioned in the house on April 8, 1965, I consider that the major reform, better than any other, would be to provide for the replacement of trustees according to the needs of each bankruptcy district by one or more competent and specialized civil servants who would be well paid and whose sole purpose or interest would be to settle the bankruptcy submitted to them as efficiently and quickly as possible. In my
6500

June 16, 1966
Bankruptcy Act
opinion, when that essential improvement to the full application of the act is made, a considerable decrease of all bankruptcies, both legal or illegal, will be noted.
In this regard I refer to the Mercier report respecting trustees which speaks about the conflict of interest of the trustee who acts for the bankrupt, his client, and for the creditors, he has the responsibility to protect.
Mr. Chairman, if we do not accept this means, which is the best in my opinion, if we do not want to go that far, the act should be amended so that the creditors, in practice as in principle, may appoint the trustees in bankruptcies and proposals. As a rule, the creditors would then appoint reliable persons, trustees who have a good reputation. This act contains considerable improvements in this respect, in clause 5 and the following, particularly as far as bankruptcy proposals are concerned. At present, the debtor chooses the trustee in proposals, when he should be appointed by the official receiver after consulting with the main creditors. Besides, the proposal should first be filed with the receiver.
In the case of assignments, subsection 4 of section 26 of the present Bankruptcy Act provides this method of appointment of the trustee, but it is seldom applied as far as I know.
Consultation of the main creditors for the selection of the trustee should be compulsory since, once he has been chosen, the trustee is practically irremovable at the present time.
Mr. Chairman, it would take too much time to mention all the amendments which should be made to the Bankruptcy Act and I will only briefly comment on certain important clauses of this bill. The present legislation gives in fact a right and power of control to the creditors, especially to the inspectors appointed by them. They are often the first to blame, if they do not keep sustained interest in a bankruptcy or do not take the necessary means to discover and punish the fraud.
But in most cases the assets are not extensive and creditors are not ready to spend their own money to try to recover part of it in such a dubious way. Public authorities must therefore intervene to make the necessary inquiries. This legislation gives extraordinary powers to the superintendent to undertake inquiries not only about each bankrupt, but even before the filing of a petition in bankruptcy, if fraud is suspected.
In addition, clause 16 empowers the receiver to make an inquiry and compels the

trustee to submit certain reports. Those are major improvements which should give results if they are strictly and generally enforced as I hope they will be. The present legislation does not make a proper distinction concerning transactions made before the bankruptcy, at arm's length, to use the recognized expression, between related persons or a corporation, its representatives or shareholders. The Department of National Revenue has succeeded in defining the term and in making it specific in the Income Tax Act, thus substantially reducing the resulting loss of revenue. This bill should correct these situations, often technically legal, but not covered by what is commonly referred to as straightforward commercial practices.
Clauses 5 and 9 of the bill have brought material improvements to proposals made by insolvent persons, providing for the appointment of inspectors, and when a proposal is not accepted by the creditors, assimilating it to an assignment. At the present time, an insolvent person may, for several weeks, postpone any legal action simply by filing any proposal with a trustee. The provision under which a trustee must require the bankrupt to deposit part of his income for instance, upon request of a creditor, should also correct certain abuses, particularly in the case of personal bankruptcies.
Also amended, Mr. Chairman, and rightly so, were sections 114 and 115 concerning the summary administration of estates, that is where the assets are under $500, the summary administration which in the past, gave rise to notorious abuses. Such changes should assuredly make for a better administration of small estates. For my part, I think summary administration procedure should be provided for only in cases where unsecured liabilities are less than, let us say, $20,000.
These are the main changes to the Bankruptcy Act mentioned in Bill No. S-17 and I shall not deal with part X, or nearly one third of the bill, bearing on the methodical payment of debts, because it will apply only to the provinces that wish it. Since the province of Quebec already has similar legislation, I doubt that "la belle province" will request that it be applied within its territory.
Mr. Chairman, many other suggestions could be made for the improvement of the present deplorable situation, but I am sure this is an important step in the right direction, until the complete revision of the act can be commented upon, which, I hope, will not be too long delayed.
June 16. 1966

Mr. Chairman, before closing I have one word for the Minister of Justice who mentioned a while ago that he was considering transferring to the Exchequer Court the jurisdiction of bankruptcy cases. Without having gone deeply into the matter, I have some reservations to make at first glance, because a considerable extension to the Exchequer Court would be required, while we already have in all bankruptcy districts Superior Court Justices who are generally competent and who, at home, at least administer quite properly the bankruptcy legislation, and there are no undue delays and the cases are being heard. Besides, the fault lies not with the judicial administration of the Bankruptcy Act but rather in the enforcement of the act itself.
At any rate, I hope that we shall have the opportunity to comment on this point in particular when the overall reviewing of the Bankruptcy Act is soon before us.

I do not want to refer to the clauses in detail but clause 21 introduces a new part X into the act dealing with the orderly payment of debts. There is a series of new sections 173 to 198, dealing with this matter. I believe the same proposal was in a Senate bill a few years ago.
Here is the problem I want to put to the minister. As I understand it, the authority of the federal parliament to deal with this subject rests in section 91 under the heading of bankruptcies and insolvencies. I do not believe we have any right to deal with what would normally be civil rights unless they come within the purview of bankruptcy and insolvency. The proposed section 173 defines a debtor as not including a corporation. However, in no way is part X restricted to insolvent or bankrupt debtors. In theory, therefore, any debtor, whether insolvent or otherwise, who comes within the definition and who wants to apply for a consolidation order with respect to his debts, would have

June 16, 1966
Bankruptcy Act
the right to apply. The Bankruptcy Act itself defines debtor in section 2, subsection (i). This definition includes an insolvent person.
In other words, what I am suggesting to the minister is that, unless you include somewhere in the definition a clause making it clear that it is an insolvent debtor who is being dealt with, you run the grave risk of some court saying these arrangements you have made are invalid because you are going beyond the field of insolvency. I know there have been cases which have dealt with the problem of provincial legislation which extended into the field of bankruptcy and insolvency. This legislation was not good legislation according to the court decision. I suggest there is a real danger of the converse here. I believe it is important to small, personal debtors to have this right to have their debts consolidated. The legislation is very practical and worth while, so I would not want to see it fall because of legal or technical grounds.
It may be that the minister has had this matter looked into and has received opinions. I do not profess to have studied the matter in great detail. However, I recall that when it came up before I had similar feelings of doubt. I wonder whether it could be looked into? I believe the difficulty could be cured simply by having a definition of debtor in this part. There is already a definition of debtor which excludes a corporation. We could make it clear the provision applies to insolvents. It could be defined very clearly to bring them within the act by referring to people who do not pay their debts. After all, we are all debtors in these days of credit. If the definition is too broad you may run into a constitutional objection.

I am thinking of a bankruptcy which has occurred because of misfortune or because of action completely beyond the control of the insolvent person. These provisions do in fact provide that salaries, wages and so on cannot exactly be confiscated but at least there can be some claim made on them after the bankruptcy. I wish the minister to know that we are concerned about this. No doubt there have been cases where there has been a wrongful transfer of assets which has contributed to income after the bankruptcy and certainly this income should be included in the assets to which the creditors have access. But there is no distinction made in this section except that the court may make a determination having regard to family responsibilities and so on. When this is put into law it will provide a means whereby wages, salaries and so on of an insolvent person can be claimed after the bankruptcy.
I think this is quite a wide departure from what we have considered in the past to be the end of an insolvent situation by reason of all the assets of the individual having been distributed at the time of the bankruptcy. Mr. Chairman, with regard to clause 10, which says-
-an order directing the payment to the trustee of such part of the salary, wages or other remuneration as the court may determine having regard to the family responsibilities and personal situation of the bankrupt.
I respectfully submit to the minister that this wording seems much too vague and gives a lot of leeway indeed. There is some kind of legislation-at least in the province of Quebec -which provides a limit on the portion of a salary to be garnisheed and, of course, the phrase-
-having regard to the family responsibilities and personal situation of the bankrupt.
-often means, in some cases, that no part of the salary shall be garnisheed.
The principle in itself is that a bankrupt, even though of good faith, has made his creditors lose money and must just the same pay them back with part of his salary. In principle, I do not think that anyone can object to that, but how will the bankrupt's family responsibilities and the personal situation be taken into account. I respectfully submit that such a text must be sufficiently clear and must not come into conflict with other legislation where it is stipulated that part of the salary can be garnisheed.
Moreover, in that regard, I respectfully submit that a maximum should be set. For instance, in the case of a bankruptcy where 25 or 50 per cent of the debts have been paid, I wonder if it is necessary then to institute proceedings against a debtor who failed in business in good faith and who would still be forced to give away the part of his salary subject to garnishee. It seems to me that when a debtor has met his obligations, at least to a great extent, steps should be taken to prevent part of his salary from being garnisheed, according precisely to the proportions set in that case. I think that, in general, that text is too vague and must be linked to certain standards, maximums and minimums within which something could be done.

Mr. Chairman, in this corner some have objected to clause 10, particularly because they thought that personal bankrupts did not constitute a problem in Canada, and I see that the Superintendent of Bankruptcy has produced statistics showing that, from 1955 to 1964, personal bankrupts had

doubled in Canada and that it constituted a major problem. I think so too.
At the present time, the bankrupt can be required to deposit with the trustee a certain portion of his salary, but unfortunately he very seldom does, and creditors have to apply to the court for an order directing the bankrupt to deposit with the trustee the portion of his salary subject to garnishee.
But the bill is noiy doing away with that procedure and the trustee will have to apply to the court for an order to this effect and this, of course, will not prevent the bankrupt from requesting his discharge at a given time.
Therefore, I do not agree with the hon. member who dealt with this matter and I think this section should remain as it now appears in the act.

Mr. Chairman, we are of course concerned with both sides of the coin, and I wonder whether it would be helpful to explain how the department has looked at this problem. We feel that in this way the trustee would be, if directed by the inspector or the creditors, obliged to apply to the court to decide whether the bankrupt should pay the trustee for the benefit of the creditor a certain portion of his income, whatever the source. The courts have held that by the effect of section 39A(3)(b) such portion of the salary that is subject to that procedure by legal process is vested in the trustee. This, however, does not apply to future and personal earnings which are not of a fixed sum. The amendment we are now bringing forward will correct this.
Similar judgments have also held that all of the seizable portion of the salary of a bankrupt is vested with the trustee and that the courts have no jurisdiction in that respect. The amendment will give some discretion to the courts in respect of the portion of the income to be deposited with the trustee, which will be set by the courts having regard to the family responsibility and personal situation of the bankrupt.
I understand there has been considerable abuse in this area in the past and it was felt
June 16, 1966

that if a portion of the salary was made con-tributable to the bankruptcy it would indeed be very helpful. On the other hand, in order to avoid abuses in this area the court would have to make sure that no abuse was perpetrated in either direction.

Mr. Chairman, I do not take any more exception to the clause than I have taken but, as the hon. member for Broadview said, it involves an entirely new concept so far as the Bankruptcy Act is concerned. There is no question that when there is fraud, gross negligence or anything of that nature which contributed to the bankruptcy some justification exists for taking this action. In relation to what the hon. member for Yukon has said, we are as anxious as any other group in this house to make changes in the Bankruptcy Act so that these fraudulent practices can be dealt with adequately, but there is nothing in the new proposed section 39A which states that this provision shall only be applied where fraud, gross negligence and so on are indicated. I am not saying the provision will always apply because there is a discretionary power in so far as the courts are concerned, but there is nothing to prevent it from being applied in all cases where there is fraud and negligence involved.
I am not going to take any further exception to the clause, but I think the application of this new section must be handled very carefully so it will not be used in violation of what has been regarded as the proper application of the law in respect of bankruptcies.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to speak again on this clause because I think that here is a clear indication of some of the difficulties incurred in the drafting of this bill, and of the difficulties which will be faced in the operating of The Company of Young Canadians.
As I stated on Friday afternoon of last week, clause 10 contains a conflict in philosophy that is somewhat crucial. I am not sure whether all hon. members have yet realized what a unique and novel bill this is. In effect it is going to provide for a highly independent corporation. Although I am not an experienced parliamentarian, I know of no other bill setting up a corporation in which two thirds of the members of its board of directors are to be appointed, not by the governor in council but in this instance by the volunteers and members of the agency itself. This is the genius of the program, that we are giving a tremendous amount of autonomy to The Company of Young Canadians.
I have been assured by youth leaders and workers that without this autonomy the program could not receive the wholehearted support of youth. I am only too well aware of the dangers inherent in youth organizations which are overtly controlled by other outside and perhaps more senior bodies, and it is on that ground I disagree with the conflict in philosophy contained in clause 10. We are trying to say something clearly but it does not come through. It has to be said clearly in this clause, as indeed throughout the whole bill, that the board will have a high degree of autonomy and that the executive director, who will be the most important person in this program, will be ultimately responsible to the board of directors of The Company of Young Canadians. Unless we say that clearly we put the whole program in great jeopardy. If we do not say it, then we asserting that we are not anxious to give these young people the trust they both want and need in order to formulate this highly exciting program. Therefore I sincerely ask the government to consider adding the words "and with the concurrence of the council" after the words "during pleasure" in subclause (1). This will give assurance with respect to the authority to whom the executive director will be responsible, and will leave no doubt in the minds of the board of directors.
[The Chairman.]

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT

Mr. Chairman, I support the contention that there is an ambiguity in the clause. If it is the intention of the drafters of the legislation that the executive director shall be appointed on the recommendation of the council of The Company of Young Canadians, then it should be followed through logically, and the authority for replacement should rest with the council of the company. As the clause stands, it would seem that this is something left to the discretion of the governor in council.
As has been said by previous speakers, and most notably by the hon. member for Prince, if youth is to participate in this program to the full extent that we all hope they will, it must be made abundantly clear in the legislation that the organization and direction of the program is left with them so far as possible, in fact to the ultimate degree possible. This ambiguity could be dealt with easily by incorporating the proposed amendment suggested by the previous speaker.

The advice of the Department of Justice is very clear, that by the same token the executive director may lose his employment on the action of the governor in council upon the recommendation of the council. In other words, the council of The Company of Young Canadians can recommend to the governor in council that the executive director be fired.

It is an act to incorporate a company or corporation which is not an agent of Her Majesty; that is provided under clause 20. It will be noted that the company shall be deemed to be a charitable organization in Canada; that is provided for by clause 22.
There has been a line of cases which have been carefully considered in the drafting of this bill. It has been decided, both in the Supreme Court and in the Privy Council, that companies incorporated by the dominion under the Companies Act-now corporations-or by a special act of parliament have all the powers given to theta by their charters or acts of incorporation, and may exercise those powers consistently with sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act. These corporations, according to the judicial decisions, are subject to provincial laws of general application, such as laws imposing taxes, or relating to mortmain, or requiring licenses for certain purposes, and so on.
My hon. and learned friend will recall the relevance in this matter of the Great West Saddlery Company Limited case of 1921 and the John Deere Plow Company v. Wharton case of 1915.
Dealing more specifically with the constitutionality of the bill with regard to education, we find that private acts incorporating religious orders and their power to teach have been passed at different times by parliament without any question ever being raised as to the validity of the legislation. In 1957 we incorporated the Oblate Fathers of Assumption Province, and among the powers granted we find in section 7 that-

Because, these days, young people ask for aU sorts of things. On the other hand, they have all kinds of organizations. For instance, local organizations, social organizations, community centres; they have the chambers of commerce, the junior and the senior, through which countless requests are made to both provincial and federal governments.
Even now, the governments cannot meet all the requests. Why then should another company be set up with its new bureaucracy costing Canadians millions which will render but few services? If we could afford it, then I might say: perhaps. But as the whole matter is properly provincial, I feel it should be left to the provinces themselves to deal with. I feel the federal government should not butt in where it has no business. We should take care of our business and let the provinces mind theirs. The federal government should not trespass in every sphere of provincial jurisdiction.
The provinces know what they want. The only thing they want, the only thing they need also, the wherewithal.
Let us work toward the setting up of a financial system that will reflect the physical potential of the country. There is a tremendous physical potential, as you know, and it is the reason why it is desired to set up such a body. But, if the financial potential is lacking, then the physical potential is unavailable. It is our duty to organize the financial possibilities to meet the demands of these agencies. As you are aware, the needs are not being met satisfactorily. There are a lot of things which we could do, but our financial means do not allow us to do so. Thus, instead of going ahead, we remain at a standstill, we do nothing. What is the good of creating other agencies which require more financial means, if we are unable to settle that problem.
Let us begin with this main problem, which is factor number one of the whole economic structure and, afterwards, the other factors can be settled. In fact, the other factors will be settled automatically.
The only thing missing in Canada, as everyone knows, is the financial power to realize what we have to realize, to develop what we have to develop. The young people know that there are natural resources to develop, they build great hopes on natural resources, but they know that we are not able to develop them ourselves, that they have to be developed by foreigners. We have to accept

foreign capital and we remain simple workers, simple water-carriers.
This is not the only problem to settle, the setting-up of this new company, the so-called company of young Canadians; there are many other factors and many other problems to settle, and as long as you do not get at the root of the problem, things will go as they are going now, backwards. And foreigners will develop our wealth and we will take what is left.
Last year, profits of two billion dollars were made by various companies, and these profits went beyond our border. Those two billion dollars, we do not have them. If we owned our wealth and resources, we would have two billion dollars more to put into circulation, two billion dollars to meet needs and demands.
Let us open our eyes. It is possible to settle these matters, but you will never settle them otherwise than through the financial economy of the country, never otherwise.
The young people do not want piles of debts and piles of taxes; they want the common heritage which is theirs. They want to have that. But they are not interested in piles of debts and piles of taxes that are made and continue to be made.
Hence, the organization of The Company of Young Canadians does not interest the young, it interests above all those in politics, those who are trying to make political capital for the next general election.
