Mr. Speaker, on Monday, June 6, and again on Wednesday, June 8, I put questions to the Prime Minister concerning the announced intention to have a national defence headquarters building erected a few blocks west of Parliament Hill in such a manner that it would tower over the Peace Tower of this building. On the first occasion the Prime Minister indicated that he would take my question as notice. On the second occasion he said he was having an examination made of the comparative measurements of the two buildings.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
I should like at the outset of these very serious remarks that I wish to make, to indicate that I have got as much information as I could regarding these buildings, and I should like to put the information on record. I understand that the height of the Peace Tower, from its base to the top of the tower, is 296 feet. The information given us concerning the proposed national defence headquarters is that the height of the building from the ground to the top would be 460 feet. In terms of the two buildings as such, therefore, the proposed national defence building would be 164 feet taller than the Peace Tower on Parliament hill. However, as everyone knows, the Le Breton Flats area west of parliament hill where it is proposed to erect the national defence building is lower than the elevation of parliament hill, and this fact must be taken into consideration.
June 16. 1966

I have endeavoured to get the facts as to the comparative elevations of these two locations. In the main I was able to get my information from the engineers' branch or the surveyor's office of the city of Ottawa. Before I did that I discovered, as most members know, that there is a bench-mark tablet on the side of the Peace Tower, placed there by the geodetic survey of Canada, which indicates that the height above sea level at the point of that bench-mark is 293.959 feet.
However, that bench-mark is a few feet above ground level, so one has to ascertain the level at the base of the tower and that level, according to the information I got from the city of Ottawa, is 281 feet above sea level. On the other hand, the elevation at the corner of Fleet and Booth Streets down in Le Breton Flats, at approximately where I understand the defence tower is to be built, is 184 feet. In other words, that area out there is 97 feet lower than the point where the Peace Tower rises from the ground. So, one has to deduct that 97 feet from the difference between the height of the buildings themselves, which is 164 feet, and this leaves a net difference in elevation above sea level of 67 feet. In other words, the proposed national defence tower would rise 67 feet higher than the Peace Tower on this building.
I urge very strongly, Mr. Speaker, that reconsideration be given to this proposal. I do so for several reasons and I can only give them in the form of headings. First of all, I think there is a symbolism that should be considered. I believe that the Peace Tower of this building represents the civil authority of government in this country, and in my view it should be higher than the tower that would represent the military authority. I believe it is appropriate that the tower that graces this hill is known by the name of the Peace Tower, and I think a tower dedicated to peace should be a taller structure than the tower of a building built for the purposes of national defence.
I also believe there are aesthetic reasons to take into account. I think the skyline of the city of Ottawa is something of which we can be proud. I submit one of the elements in it that gives us pride is the Peace Tower on parliament hill. If the proposed national defence tower were being built two, three or four miles away from parliament hill the arguments that I advance might not
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion apply, but a tower that is only to be a few blocks away, rising higher than the Peace Tower, would detract from the Peace Tower and spoil the skyline of the city of Ottawa. I have looked at it a number of times since I raised this question by driving in from various directions and I believe we would regret very much if this skyline and the beauty we have here were spoiled in this way.
I think that a government that is in power for only a short time, even a parliament that is here for only a short time, has to be careful when it takes a course of action that has an effect for decades, perhaps for half a century, or for a century to come. We are not erecting something that can be torn down by the next parliament or the next government. We are erecting something that will stay, and we ought to think carefully about such a course of action before it is proceeded with.
There are many other questions that could be raised. There is the question of the huge cost involved. Some of my friends to my right are raising that. There are questions respecting the need for so much space, and there are questions of military strategy. It seems to me rather strange that the defence headquarters would be put so close to the parliament buildings themselves. But at any rate while all these arguments are part of the story and should be considered, in the main I think the symbolism is the most important factor and it should not be overlooked.
Mr. Speaker, one newspaper in an editorial against me on this matter says that I am living in the past and asks if I do not realize that skyscrapers reflect progress. I think the story of the Tower of Babel gives the answer to that. I hope we are not going to build another one.

CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-POSSIBLE VIOLATION OF ACT IN PUBLIC AFFAIRS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the point I wanted to raise tonight refers to the Broadcasting Act, Chapter 22, Statutes of Canada, 1958.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey)-whom I do not want to attack meanly for, on the contrary, I consider him as a gentleman-recently took part in a French program better known as "Les Affaires de l'Etat", or "The Nation's Business" in English. I hold nothing against him personally, but rather against the C.B.C. on the one hand, and the Conservative party, on the other, who, in my opinion, were guilty of a glaring violation of the Broadcasting Act.
Section 17 says:
No licensee shall broadcast in dramatized form any program, advertisement or announcement of a partisan political character.
And a little further section 29, subsection 2, reads as follows:
The Corporation is bound by the provisions of Part 1,
which includes section 17 that I have just quoted.
Now, Mr. Speaker, first I want to remark that the Broadcasting Act is obsolete. It should undergo a thorough revision for it is archaic and contains provisions which are difficult to apply and make it something like the old Quebec liquor act, an hypocritical law, because one could not do otherwise than break it.
The Broadcasting Act states first of all, as I was saying, that political broadcast shall not be dramatized. But the act does not define dramatization. We do not know exactly what it means.
For instance, the mere fact that the Leader of the Opposition will be there is enough to lend a dramatic character to a program, for he has the knack of dramatizing everything.
Therefore, would the Leader of the Opposition's participation in a program warrant its cancellation? This would present a problem difficult to solve.
But when the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi appeared on that program, instead of dealing with politics, as is usually the case on that program, he described at length a
June 16. 1966	COMMONS
member of parliament in action, and during his narrative, the opera voice of the hon. member was heard against a musical background all through the program. So, instead of an informative program, it turned out to be a play, where the hon. member was seen at various meetings, or going around his riding chatting with farmers, attending a horse auction, motoring in a convertible in his shirt sleeves. In other words, if that is not dramatization of a political program, I think we will never be able to define what dramatization is. From that point of view, I think the act should be revised because, as I said, it is obsolete.
Second, another provision of the act states that the sponsor and the political party must be identified. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this tends to commercialize political programs which should be on a higher plane and really be informative.
The Broadcasting Act says that there shall be no program of a partisan political character on any day that an election is held in the municipal, provincial or federal field. It does not say whether a program dealing with federal politics may be put on the air while a municipal election is being held. There is something illogical and indefinite in the act. It will have to be revised.
Finally, the act says that no broadcast of a partisan political character shall take place within 48 hours of an election. I think, Mr. Chairman, that this is going a little too far. A 24-hour time limit would be more like it. I believe it would be adequate since the politicians taking part in those programs must necessarily have a sense of responsibility and they cannot use texts of a defamatory character on account of the censorship; besides, such a censorship is required by the Board of Broadcast Governors.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make another suggestion, that is all private stations should be compelled to do like the C.B.C. and give the opportunity to all political parties to be heard.
What is now happening for example, in the province of Quebec is that channel 10 has a much higher rating than the C.B.C. In Quebec city, channel 4, which is a private station, has also a much higher rating than the C.B.C. Then it is difficult to reach the public through the C.B.C.

If private stations were compelled, pursuant to the Broadcasting Act, to make time available to political parties as the C.B.C is compelled to do, I think that the situation would be improved.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would ask the minister representing the government: Will there be an investigation and will legal action be taken against the C.B.C. which, with the complicity of the Conservative party, has infringed the Broadcasting Act?
If the government fails to take action, if there is no investigation, then I should advise the minister that I shall personally and shortly take legal action against the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for having openly violated the provisions of section 17 of the Broadcasting Act, in a broadcast in which the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi took part, who has surely behaved like one of the hosts of "Les Couche-Tard" or as a member of the "Cre-Basile" show, instead of having regard for the informative character that must be maintained in a political broadcast.
I should like to know from the minister whether there has been an investigation or whether additional measures should be taken.
